name: Calcipotriol

card.summary: A topical vitamin D analog prescribed for plaque psoriasis, clearing scaly patches so skin looks smoother and more even.
card.note: Not for use on the face per standard contraindications; can irritate skin.

quick.overview:
Calcipotriol is a synthetic derivative of calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D, applied to the skin to treat plaque psoriasis. It is a prescription medicine sold as Dovonex, Daivonex or Psorcutan.

It helps appearance by reducing the thick, red, scaly plaques of psoriasis, leaving clearer skin. It is also available combined with the corticosteroid betamethasone.
quick.how: Applied topically to affected areas as prescribed, alone or in a fixed-dose combination with betamethasone. It is a long-term psoriasis treatment, and results are judged over weeks.
quick.risks: Very common effects are burning, itching and irritation; rare ones include hypercalcaemia, photosensitivity, pigment change, skin thinning and allergic contact dermatitis. Contraindications include hypersensitivity, use on the face, hypercalcaemia and vitamin D toxicity.[1]

lead: Calcipotriol, also called calcipotriene, is a synthetic vitamin D derivative used topically for plaque psoriasis. It was patented in 1985, approved for medical use in 1991 and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1]

It binds the vitamin D receptor about as strongly as calcitriol while having much weaker effects on calcium; its exact antipsoriatic mechanism is not fully understood, and a proposed explanation is calming overactive T cells.[1] Clearing plaques improves how affected skin looks.
Randomised trial work has also combined calcipotriol with 5-fluorouracil for skin-cancer precursors.[6][12] Wikipedia mentions use in alopecia areata based on a single case report.[1]

chain: Topical vitamin D analog applied to plaques
Slows overactive skin-cell turnover and inflammation
Thinner, less red, less scaly patches
angle.text: Calcipotriol is used to treat psoriasis plaques, which improves how affected skin looks. It is applied directly to the patches.

paras: Chronic plaque psoriasis is its chief use.[1] Reviews and trials cover plaque and guttate psoriasis and childhood psoriasis.[3][10][9]
Appearance interest centres on clearing visible psoriasis patches. Wikipedia notes an alopecia areata case report, but no larger trial was found.[1]
Burning, itching and irritation are very common; dermatitis, dryness, redness and peeling are common; rare effects include hypercalcaemia, photosensitivity, pigmentation changes and skin atrophy.[1]
It is metabolised in the liver and excreted in bile, with little skin absorption.[1]

Trials include a randomised trial of calcipotriol plus 5-fluorouracil for skin-cancer precursors, a systematic review on guttate psoriasis, and a systematic review of the calcipotriol/5-FU combination in actinic keratosis, Bowen's disease and squamous cell carcinoma.[6][3][12] Older trials examined psoriasis treatment and childhood use.[9][10]
